title: Failed Head and Shoulders / Rounded Top
teaches: The failed head-and-shoulders as we trade it, the long: a leader above its 200-day draws the top everyone sees, the neckline breaks and the fall stays shallow and is bought back (or the break never comes), the buy is the first trade over the right-shoulder high at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low while the undercut low is only the invalidation line, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a whipsaw loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: A strong rally, climaxing a more or less extensive advance, on which trading volume becomes very heavy
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: the left shoulder comes at the climax of an extensive advance.

facts.quote: A third rally, but this time on decidedly less volume than accompanied the formation of either the left shoulder or the head, which fails to reach the height of the head
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: the right shoulder is a third rally that fails to reach the head's height.

facts.quote: Until the neckline is broken, a certain percentage of Head-and-Shoulders developments, perhaps 20%, are "saved"
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: perhaps 20% of tops are saved before the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: A Head-and-Shoulders Formation that does not work is a warning that even though there is still some life in the situation, a genuine turn is near.
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: a failed top is a warning that a real turn is near.

facts.quote: It pictures simply and plainly a gradual, progressive, and fairly symmetrical change in the trend direction, produced by a gradual shift in the balance of power between buying and selling.
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: a rounding turn is a gradual, symmetrical change of trend.

facts.quote: Until that downside violation takes place, however, there is always the pos¬ sibility that the pattern is not really a head and shoulders top and that the uptrend may resume at some point.
facts.claim: Murphy: until the neckline breaks, the uptrend may simply resume.

facts.quote: This might be sufficient cause to liquidate long positions, but not necessarily enough to justify new short sales.
facts.claim: Murphy: the topping signs justify selling longs, not new shorts.

facts.quote: At a top, once the neckline has been broken on the down¬ side, any decisive close back above the neckline is a serious warn¬ ing that the initial breakdown was probably a bad signal
facts.claim: Murphy: a decisive close back over the neckline says the breakdown was a bad signal.

facts.quote: probably the best known and most reliable of all major reversal patterns
facts.claim: Murphy: the head and shoulders is the best known reversal pattern.

facts.quote: Without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a Head and Shoulders reversal pattern (or any reversal pattern, for that matter).
facts.claim: StockCharts: no prior uptrend, no head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: The head and shoulders pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend is not reversed until the neckline support is broken.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the top is not complete until the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: Sometimes, but certainly not always, the price will return to the support break and offer a second chance to sell.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the return move to the broken neckline is a second chance to sell.

facts.quote: While symmetry is preferred, sometimes the shoulders can be out of whack.
facts.claim: StockCharts: symmetry is preferred, not required.

facts.quote: A three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: three peaks, the middle one highest.

facts.quote: The two shoulders should peak near the same price, be nearly the same distance from the head, and look similar
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the two shoulders should peak near the same price.

facts.quote: Wait for confirmation before placing a trade.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: wait for confirmation before trading the top.

facts.quote: breaks out downward and drops no more than 10%, turns around, and then closes above the top of the head-and-shoulders
facts.claim: Bulkowski's busted top: a break that drops no more than 10% and turns around.

facts.quote: To trade this busted chart pattern, place a buy order a penny above the head (the highest high in the chart pattern).
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys the busted top a penny above the head.

facts.quote: 30% of them will triple bust
facts.claim: Bulkowski: 30% of busted tops triple bust, so failures whipsaw.

facts.quote: A busted pattern occurs when price breaks out in one direction and moves less than 10% away from the breakout price
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a bust moves less than 10% from the breakout price before reversing.

facts.quote: Prices form a gentle curve, a half moon shape.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rounding top is a gentle half-moon curve.

facts.quote: A close above the highest high signals an upward breakout. Downward breakouts are a close below the lower of the two rims (the lowest low in the pattern).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rounding top breaks up over its highest high and down under the lower rim.

facts.quote: Heavy breakout volume suggests better performance.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: heavy breakout volume suggests better performance.

facts.quote: Tall patterns perform better than short ones.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: tall patterns perform better than short ones.

facts.quote: The advance today, May 18, penetrated the May 10 right shoulder high and officially completed the failure pattern.
facts.claim: Brandt: the failure pattern completes when price penetrates the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: The market should probably not take out Wednesday's low (652-3/4).
facts.claim: Brandt's line in the sand was the trigger day's low.

facts.quote: I consider H&S failure patterns to be very tradable chart developments.
facts.claim: Brandt: H&S failures are very tradable.

facts.quote: The target of 733 is based on projecting the distance between the April 26 high and the May 12 low (which is 69 cents) upward from the right shoulder high of 664.
facts.claim: Brandt's target: the head-to-post-break-low distance added to the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: Unfortunately novice market analysts are way to quick to mislabel market action as a H&S configuration.
facts.claim: Brandt: novices mislabel ordinary action as a head and shoulders.

facts.quote: It is not unusual for H&S tops to be brief, whereas H&S bottom patterns tend to be much longer in duration.
facts.claim: Brandt: tops are often brief.

facts.quote: Remember the only way to trade a H&S pattern is to trade the failure of it.
facts.claim: Bracco: the only way to trade a head and shoulders is to trade its failure.

facts.quote: this is why coming out of corrections I try to get a position in TQQQ and SOXL.
facts.claim: Bracco uses the failed top coming out of corrections.

facts.quote: the best way to trade a head and shoulders top is to buy the failed breakdown of it.
facts.claim: Bracco: buy the failed breakdown of a head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: Turning $333 head and shoulder neckline into support is step 1. Step 2 is remounting the 50SMA and the 20EMA.
facts.claim: Bracco: neckline to support first, then remount the 50-day.

facts.quote: Failed Head and Shoulders breakdown at $325. 50SMA the line in the sand to stay above.
facts.claim: Bracco: the 50-day is the line in the sand on a failed breakdown.

facts.quote: Stop at LOD if this triggers. My stops are always LOD until I can raise them to breakeven
facts.claim: Our stop habit: the low of the day until it can go to breakeven.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if it does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit and only moves up.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: past 2R in the first 30 minutes, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day; shorts only below it.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.

facts.quote: The house meaning is the long: the breakdown everyone sees never comes, or comes and fails, and the squeeze fuels the next leg up.
facts.claim: We trade the failed top long: the squeeze fuels the next leg up.

facts.quote: The first trade above the right-shoulder high (the dome high for a rounded top) after the failure.
facts.claim: The trigger: the first trade over the right-shoulder high after the failure.

facts.quote: A few cents under the trigger day's low, with a real stop order.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the trigger day's low.

facts.quote: The low of the failed breakdown is the invalidation line, not the stop.
facts.claim: The undercut low is the invalidation line, not the stop.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a fall of more than 10% under the neckline. The top worked; this setup is gone.
facts.claim: A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked; no setup.

facts.quote: Version A (allowed, graded lower): no close under the neckline; price turns up from the right shoulder.
facts.claim: Version A: no close under the neckline; price turns up from the right shoulder; the lesser form.

facts.quote: A brief, shallow undercut (under 6% below the neckline) is the A+ form; 6% to 10% grades lower.
facts.claim: A shallow undercut under 6% is the A+ form; 6% to 10% grades lower.

facts.quote: No hard volume rule. Trigger-day volume 1.25x or more of the 50-day average is a grading plus.
facts.claim: Volume is a grade cue: 1.25x the 50-day average is a plus, never a gate.

facts.quote: The close is above the 50-day SMA on the trigger day.
facts.claim: On the trigger day the close is above the 50-day.

facts.quote: An uptrend into the pattern: the close is above a rising 200-day SMA when the left shoulder forms, and the head is at least 25% above the lowest low of the 6 months before the left shoulder.
facts.claim: Prior trend: above a rising 200-day at the left shoulder; the head at least 25% over the prior six months' low.

facts.quote: For version B the trigger comes within 40 bars of the failure; the failure itself within 60 bars of the right shoulder.
facts.claim: The trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure; the failure within 60 of the right shoulder.

facts.quote: After the buy: a close back under the neckline is a failure of the failure; the stop should already be above that.
facts.claim: After the buy, a close back under the neckline is the failure of the failure.

facts.quote: A reference, not a rule: the head is the first place sellers may return; Brandt's target is the right-shoulder high plus the distance from the head down to the post-break low.
facts.claim: The head is a reference where sellers may return, not an exit rule.

facts.quote: Grade it lower when the stock has already run for a year or more: a failed top late in a long advance can be the last push.
facts.claim: A failed top late in a long advance grades lower; it can be the last push.

facts.quote: A cue: best when the market itself is correcting or just turning up and the stock's top fails anyway, the leader refusing to break while the market falls.
facts.claim: Best when the market is correcting and the leader refuses to break.

facts.quote: Never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks, and the neckline break is not taught as a short setup
facts.claim: We never short the right shoulder before the break; the break is not a short setup here.

facts.quote: its neckline is the lower rim (the lowest low of the arc); the trigger is the dome high.
facts.claim: A rounded top's neckline is the lower rim; its trigger is the dome high.

facts.quote: A flat base holds one range 15% deep or less with a flat top tapped twice and breaks out over it; a rounded top is a dome that first broke its lower rim (or sagged toward it) and then recovered
facts.claim: A flat base is a box broken upward; a rounded top failure is a dome that lost its rim and recovered.

facts.quote: A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought the moment price reclaims that low, within 1 to 3 sessions, with the stop under the new low.
facts.claim: A 2B is one broken low bought on the reclaim within 1 to 3 sessions.

facts.quote: A failed H&S has three peaks over a neckline and waits for the trade over the right-shoulder high, with the stop under that day's low.
facts.claim: A failed H&S has three peaks over a neckline and waits for the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: A mean-reversion long buys the turn on the flush day itself, into a level, and is out in 1 to 5 sessions at the average
facts.claim: A mean-reversion long buys the flush day and is out in 1 to 5 sessions.

facts.quote: Buying the first bounce back to the neckline. That is the return move the short sellers expect; wait for the right-shoulder high.
facts.claim: A named mistake: buying the first bounce back to the neckline.

facts.quote: Using the undercut low as the stop. It is usually far more than 3% away.
facts.claim: A named mistake: the undercut low as the stop.

facts.quote: Calling every three bumps a head-and-shoulders.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling every three bumps a head and shoulders.

facts.quote: Best when the market itself is correcting and the stock refuses to break down.
facts.claim: Best when the market is correcting and the stock refuses to break down.

facts.quote: The breakdown either never comes (A) or comes, falls under 10%, and is bought back (B).
facts.claim: Version A: the break never comes. Version B: it comes, falls under 10%, and is bought back.

facts.quote: Count the tries: at most 3 in a week and 6 in a month. Failures whipsaw; a second entry over the same level is allowed.
facts.claim: Failures whipsaw; a second entry over the same level is allowed, at most 3 tries a week.

facts.quote: If the stop is more than about 3% under the entry, size it down to the risk or skip.
facts.claim: A stop wider than about 3%: size down to the risk or skip.

facts.quote: A Green or Yellow reading (F65); in Orange, A+ only.
facts.claim: Green or Yellow; in Orange, A+ only.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a close under the 200-day.
facts.claim: A close under the 200-day before the trigger ends the setup.

facts.quote: The failure fails: price closes back under the neckline and the top works after all (Bulkowski's double bust), or the trigger whipsaws through a tight day-low stop before the real move (AAPL 2026).
facts.claim: The failure mode: the failure fails, or the trigger whipsaws through the day-low stop before the real move.

facts.quote: The close is above the 200-day SMA on the trigger day (hard).
facts.claim: The close is above the 200-day on the trigger day, a hard rule.

facts.quote: A market order once price is through the level, during regular hours.
facts.claim: A market order once price is through the level, in regular hours.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.
facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.

facts.quote: A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up.
facts.claim: A real stop order with the broker; it only moves up.

facts.quote: Chasing a gap far over the right shoulder (LULU 2023, 11.4%).
facts.claim: A named mistake: chasing a gap far over the right shoulder.

facts.quote: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
facts.claim: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out past 2R.

facts.quote: Time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.
facts.claim: Under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: The position is at most 1% of average daily volume.
facts.claim: The position is at most 1% of average daily volume.

facts.quote: Price $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day on average.
facts.claim: Price $10 or more and $20 million a day or more.

facts.quote: a failed H&S waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back and then for the trade over the right-shoulder high, and holds for a trend.
facts.claim: A failed H&S waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back, then holds for a trend.

facts.quote: Version B (preferred): at least one close under the neckline, or an intraday undercut of the right armpit low, that does not fall more than 10% under the neckline before the trigger.
facts.claim: Version B: a close under the neckline, or an undercut of the right armpit low, bought back before falling 10%.

facts.quote: At entry, no more than 10% above the 9 EMA.
facts.claim: At entry, no more than 10% above the 9 EMA.

facts.quote: Forgetting Edwards and Magee's warning: a failed top late in a long advance can be the last push (GOOGL 2026).
facts.claim: A named mistake: forgetting that a late failed top can be the last push.

facts.quote: Sell a third at 3R.
facts.claim: Sell a third at 3R.

facts.quote: Sell a third at 5R.
facts.claim: Sell a third at 5R.

facts.quote: If it opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.claim: MGM: shoulders within 0.3%, a flat neckline, a four-week failed breakdown, a trigger on 1.9x volume.

facts.claim: BXP: level shoulders, a flat neckline, a two-week undercut, a trigger above the 50-day.

facts.claim: MCO: the trigger day gapped 1% over the level, bought at the open inside the chase limit, on 2.6x volume.

facts.quote: The shallow version: the head only 9% over the neckline and a one-day, 1% undercut. Teaches that the failure can be small.

facts.claim: ICLR: triggered on 1.0x volume, 3R took three weeks, then a 25% run; no volume spike needed.

walkthroughs.title: MGM, September 2004: the symmetrical top that failed
steps: MGM, 2004. A head and shoulders everyone can see: shoulders within 0.3% of each other, a flat neckline at 21.22.
It breaks, falls 6.1% under the neckline, and the shorts lean in. Four weeks later the break is bought back.
September 14 it trades over the right shoulder, 22.70, on 1.9 times volume. Buy at market, 22.71. Stop 22.30, under the low.
A close back under the neckline and the top's working after all. Instead 3R came in 5 days, 23.7R at best.

walkthroughs.title: SPG, November 2005: the invalidation line is not the stop
steps: Here's why the low isn't your stop. SPG, 2005: three peaks, the head 12.4% over a 65.03 neckline.
The break runs seven weeks, down to 61.03. Lose that and the top's worked. But it's way too far to risk against.
November 11, back over the 50-day, it trades over the right shoulder, 69.52. Buy at market, 69.53. Stop 68.76, 1.1% away.
A close back under 65.03 is the failure failing. Instead 3R came in 6 days, 11.9R at best.

walkthroughs.title: MUSA, March 2022: the leader that refused to break
steps: Early 2022, the market's correcting. MUSA builds a head and shoulders and breaks 6.8% under its 176.18 neckline.
Three weeks later it's bought back, with the market still falling. A leader refusing to break. That's the best setting.
March 15 it trades over the right shoulder, 184.96. Buy at market, 184.97. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 182.98.
3R the next day. Stop to breakeven and let it run. It went on to a 40% run, 39.0R at best.

questions.q: Everyone sees this top. How do we trade it?
choices: Short it on the neckline break
questions.why: Long, once the break fails. Like Bracco says, the only way to trade a head and shoulders is to trade the failure of it. Everyone sees this top and leans short. When the break doesn't follow through, those shorts have to buy back, and that squeeze fuels the next leg up. That's the edge. ABNB here fell 3.0% under its neckline, got bought back, and the buy over the right shoulder hit 3R in 9 days. If it falls more than 10% under the neckline, the top worked and there's nothing to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Everyone sees the top. I want to be there when it fails.

wrong.Short it on the neckline break: We don't teach the break as a short. When we checked tops that formed above the 200-day, 70% of breaks were still above it, where we never short.
wrong.Short the right shoulder: Shorting before anything breaks is a guess. The uptrend can just pick back up, and we never short a right shoulder.
wrong.Long the neckline break: Buying the break is buying right into the sellers. Nothing has failed yet. Our buy waits for the trade over the right-shoulder high.

questions.simple: We buy the failure, not the break. The shorts get trapped, and their buying fuels the move up.

deeper.example: FDX, March 2003: a clean three-peak top at the 2003 bear-market bottom. The break failed in two weeks. We bought 42.98 with the stop at 42.42, 1.3% away. It reached 3R in 1 day and 17.3R at best.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-001, the direction)
fixed before

questions.story: Three peaks, the middle one highest, and the line under them has already broken. A textbook top everyone can see.

questions.q: It's back over the neckline. When do you buy it?
choices: A trade over the right-shoulder high
The first bounce back to the neckline
A touch of the undercut low
questions.answer: A trade over the right-shoulder high
questions.why: A trade over the right-shoulder high. That's the buy. Under that level the sellers can still win. Over it, everyone who sold the right shoulder is wrong, and the failure is done. MUSA did it the next session. It traded over 184.96, filled at 184.97, and hit 3R in 1 day. Mark the level the night before and set an alert, so you buy the break and don't chase it.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the right-shoulder high. The trade through it is the buy.

wrong.A touch of the undercut low: The undercut low is where the idea dies, not where it starts. It sits far under the buy.
wrong.The first bounce back to the neckline: That's the bounce the shorts wait for, their second chance to sell. Buying there is a classic mistake.
wrong.A close back over the 50-day: Getting back over the 50-day helps, but it doesn't complete anything. The buy is the right-shoulder high, during the day, never a close.

questions.simple: You buy when price trades over the right-shoulder high. A bounce back to the neckline proves nothing yet.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the trigger)
fixed before

questions.story: This top broke its neckline, but the fall stayed shallow and price climbed back over the line.

deeper.example: Peter Brandt marks it the same way. In his words, the advance through the right-shoulder high officially completed the failure pattern.

questions.q: On a failed head and shoulders, your stop goes a few cents under the low of the trigger day.
questions.why: True. A few cents under the low of the day, the LOD, on the day it triggers. That's the spot that tells you you're wrong. If price takes out the low of the day you bought, the failure isn't working. I go a few cents under rather than right on it, so a tick to the exact low doesn't knock me out. It goes in as a real stop order with your broker. The undercut low works as a stop too, but it sits much farther away. Set the stop first, then size the trade from it.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day. That's where I'm wrong.
questions.simple: True. Under the low of the trigger day is where the trade is wrong, so that's where the stop goes.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: A failed head and shoulders can be bought when the trigger day closes under the 200-day.
questions.why: False. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line. A stock under its 200-day is in a downtrend. A failed top down there is a bounce, not a new leg up. We want the close above the 200-day on the trigger day. If it isn't, pass and go find a stock that's acting right.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there's no failed top to buy. Hard line.
questions.simple: False. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so a failed top down there is a pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A head-and-shoulders top has three peaks with the ___ one highest.
questions.why: The middle one. A head-and-shoulders top is a three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others (Bulkowski). The third rally, the right shoulder, fails to reach the height of the head (Edwards and Magee). Symmetry is preferred, not required.
questions.lesson_line: Three peaks, the head in the middle, the shoulders lower on each side.
questions.simple: The middle peak is the highest, which makes it the head, and the two shoulders sit lower.

reasons: two agreeing Tier 2 sources, a stable definition

questions.q: What's that 61.03 low good for now?
choices: Your stop, a few cents under it
A spot to buy back in
questions.why: Where the idea is dead. If price ever gets back under 61.03, the top won and the setup's gone. That's your invalidation line. It's not your stop, though. It sits way too far from the buy. Here the buy was 69.53, and the low of the trigger day put the stop at 68.76, 1.1% away. When we tested it, a stop under the failed-break low sat a median 9.3% away. We like ours within about 3%, so a stop down there buys you far fewer shares for the same risk.
questions.lesson_line: The undercut low tells you when the idea is wrong. The day's low tells you when the trade is wrong.

wrong.Your stop, a few cents under it: Too far. From 61.03 up to a 69.53 buy is way past the 5% we'll ever accept, so your size shrinks to almost nothing. The stop goes under the trigger day's low.
wrong.A spot to buy back in: Price back at 61.03 means the top won. We buy over the right-shoulder high, way above it.
wrong.Your first profit target: It's under you, so it can't be a target. And the first sell is a judgment into a push, not a price off this low.

questions.simple: That low tells you when the idea is dead. It's too far away to be your stop.

deeper.example: SPG, November 2005: the break ran seven weeks down to a low of 61.03. The buy was 69.53, and the trigger day's low gave a stop of 68.76, 1.1% away. A stop at 61.03 would have been far from usable.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (the invalidation line)
fixed before

questions.story: This top broke its neckline and fell to a low of 61.03. Then buyers took it all back.

questions.q: Version B is a real neckline break that stays shallow and gets bought back.
questions.why: True. That's version B. The neckline breaks, the crowd gets its breakdown, and then it doesn't follow through. The fall stays under 10% and buyers take it back. It's the form we want, because now real sellers are trapped on the wrong side. Version A is the other kind, where the break never comes at all. If the fall goes past 10%, the top did its job and there's no failure to buy.
questions.lesson_line: A real break that gets bought back. That's the failure I want.
questions.simple: True, the neckline breaks, the fall stays small and buyers take it back. That's the version we want.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-109, versions A and B)

deeper.example: Bulkowski calls this a busted top. Price breaks down, drops no more than 10%, turns around, and closes above the top of the pattern.

questions.q: The right shoulder is forming and the neckline hasn't broken yet. What's the play?
questions.why: Nothing yet. A top that hasn't broken is just a picture. Until the neckline goes, the uptrend can simply pick back up, so shorting the shoulder is a guess. Buying is a guess too, since nothing has failed. Put it on your radar. Mark the neckline and the right-shoulder high, set alerts on both, and let price show you which way it's going.
questions.lesson_line: A top that hasn't broken is a picture, not a trade.

wrong.Short the right shoulder: We never short the right shoulder. Nothing has broken, and the uptrend can resume any day.
wrong.Buy the right shoulder: No trigger yet. You buy over the right-shoulder high after a failure, not inside the shoulder.
wrong.Buy the neckline break later: A break is the sellers winning. Our buy comes only after the break fails.

questions.simple: Wait and watch. Until the neckline breaks, the uptrend can just carry on.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-001, no short)

deeper.example: Murphy's take: the topping signs might be enough to sell longs, but not necessarily enough to justify new short sales. StockCharts says the same: the pattern isn't complete until the neckline breaks.

questions.q: A head and shoulders top only counts if there's a real uptrend in front of it.
questions.why: True. It's a reversal pattern, so it needs a run to reverse. Three bumps in a sideways stock aren't a top, they're noise. I want to see a stock that was trending, above a rising 200-day, before the shape started. That's also what makes the failure worth buying: a strong stock that shook everyone out and kept going.
questions.lesson_line: No run in front, no top. Check the trend before the shape.
questions.simple: True, a top has to reverse a run. With no uptrend in front, there's nothing to reverse.

reasons: two agreeing Tier 2 sources, a stable idea
the 25% test is our card's own number

deeper.example: StockCharts puts it simply: without a prior uptrend to reverse, there can't be a head and shoulders reversal pattern. Edwards and Magee start the pattern with a strong rally that climaxes an extensive advance.

questions.q: How do you get in?
questions.why: Market order, right now. Price is through the level during market hours, so that's your buy. Everything we buy goes in at market. A limit can sit there unfilled while the move leaves without you. A few cents of slippage is nothing next to missing the trigger. BXP did this one: through the 68.01 right-shoulder high, filled at 68.02. Have the order ready the night before so you're not fumbling at the fill.
questions.lesson_line: Through the level, in market hours, at market. No debate at the fill.

wrong.Limit order at the neckline: The neckline is way under price now. That order never fills on the trigger, and you miss the trade.
wrong.Wait and buy the close: We buy as price goes through the trigger, not at the close. By the close the fill can be much worse.
wrong.Buy premarket tomorrow: We don't buy outside regular hours. And the trigger is happening right now.

questions.simple: Buy at market right now. Price is through the level during market hours, and that's the trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.story: Yesterday it closed just under the right-shoulder high. Now it's the middle of the trading day, and price is going through that high.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After a failed breakdown, Bracco's line in the sand to stay above is the ___-day.
questions.why: 50. Bracco on the SMH failed breakdown: 50SMA the line in the sand to stay above. He calls turning the neckline into support step 1 and remounting the 50-day step 2. Our card asks for the trigger-day close above the 50-day. The 200-day is a separate and harder test: the trigger-day close must also be above it. Bracco's line here is the 50.
questions.lesson_line: Neckline to support first, then back over the 50-day. Then the trigger.
questions.simple: The answer is 50, because Bracco treats the 50-day line as the one to stay above after a failed breakdown.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion and Bracco's published posts
the 200-day is in the bank and is also a trigger-day test

questions.q: You can start a new failed-top position two days before the company reports.
questions.why: False. No new buys in the 3 days before earnings, and two days out is inside that. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, and no stop order protects you from a gap. So I'd rather wait and let the report pass. If it still sets up after, take it then. A trade you already own holds through the report only if it's up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before earnings. Let the report pass.
questions.simple: False, two days before a report is too close. A gap on the news can jump right over your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.story: A three-peak top with the right shoulder in place. Not one close comes under the neckline. Price turns up off the right shoulder and trades over its high.
questions.q: What kind of failure is this?
choices: Version B, a break bought back
Not a failed top at all
questions.why: Version A. The break everyone expected never showed up. There's no close under the neckline, and price just turned up off the right shoulder. It counts, but for now we grade it below version B. In B the sellers actually got their break and then got trapped, and that trapped selling is extra fuel. Here nobody got trapped, so there's less behind the move.
questions.lesson_line: No break, then a turn up: version A. A break that gets bought back: version B, the one I want.

wrong.Not a failed top at all: It still counts. The top got saved before the break, which is the lesser version, not nothing.
wrong.Version B, a break bought back: B needs a real close under the neckline first. This one never broke.
wrong.A 2B, a broken low reclaimed: A 2B breaks one swing low and takes it back. Nothing broke here, and there are three peaks over a neckline.

questions.simple: Version A, since the neckline never broke and price just turned up. It counts, but it's the weaker form.

deeper.counter: Version A is the common one in our data: 32,514 long-A triggers averaged +0.04R, against 6,543 for version B at +0.11R. Version A is real but thinner.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-109, versions A and B)
fixed before

questions.q: A slow, rounded dome with no single peak sticking out. Where's its neckline?
choices: The lower rim, the arc's low
The dome high, the top of the arc
A line across the two high points
questions.answer: The lower rim, the arc's low
questions.why: The lower rim, the lowest low of the arc. A rounded top has no shoulders to draw a line under, so its floor is that lowest low. That's the line the sellers need to break. If it breaks and gets bought back, that's the same failure we trade on a head and shoulders. The buy goes over the dome high.
questions.lesson_line: A dome has no shoulders. Its floor is the lower rim.

wrong.The dome high, the top of the arc: That's the ceiling, not the floor. The dome high is where the buy goes after a failure.
wrong.The 50-day moving average: A moving average is context. It isn't part of the pattern.
wrong.A line across the two high points: A dome has no two peaks to connect. Its floor is the lowest low of the arc.

questions.simple: Its neckline is the lower rim, the lowest low of the whole curve.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-002, the rounded top)
fixed before

deeper.example: Bulkowski calls a rounding top a gentle half-moon curve. He counts a downside break as a close below the lower of the two rims, the lowest low in the pattern.

questions.q: On this trade you can keep the stop in your head, as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. The stop goes in as a real order with your broker. A stop in your head turns into a debate the moment price gets there. You talk yourself into one more day, and that's how a small loss becomes a big one. A real order just does its job. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is a gap through it at the open.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False. Put a real stop order in with your broker, so it fires without a debate.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: On a version B setup, what is the longest the trigger may wait after the failure?
questions.why: 40 sessions. Our card's window for version B: the trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure, and the failure itself within 60 sessions of the right shoulder. It is a card rule for this setup, not a law of the market.
questions.lesson_line: Version B has a clock. The trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure.

wrong.10 sessions: Too tight. The card gives the trigger up to 40 sessions after the failure.
wrong.60 sessions: That is the other window: the failure itself comes within 60 sessions of the right shoulder. The trigger gets 40.
wrong.100 sessions: Too long. The card's window is 40 sessions.

questions.simple: Our card gives the trigger up to 40 sessions after the failure.

reasons: the 40 and 60 session windows are our card's proposed rule

questions.q: Head 47.22, neckline 40.82. How tall is the pattern, head to neckline, as a percent of the head?
questions.why: 13.6%. Head minus neckline, divided by the head: (47.22 - 40.82) / 47.22 = 13.6%. That is the height of FDX's 2003 top. StockCharts measures a top's height from the neckline to the top of the head.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the top from the head to the neckline, as a percent of the head.
questions.simple: The pattern is 13.6% tall: take the head minus the neckline, then divide by the head.

reasons: a computed key
fixed before

wrong.15.7%: Divided by the neckline instead of the head.
wrong.6.4%: Gave the gap in dollars as a percent, no divide.
wrong.86.4%: Gave the neckline as a share of the head.

questions.story: The day before the trigger.
The neckline broke three weeks ago. The stock is now 14% under it and still sliding.
questions.q: Still a failed head-and-shoulders candidate?
choices: Yes, once back over the neckline
No; any close below it kills it
questions.why: No. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, and this setup is gone. Bulkowski defines a bust as a break that moves less than 10% from the breakout price before it turns, and this one is 14% under. A failed head-and-shoulders is a shallow break that is bought back, not a deep slide. One close under the neckline is allowed in version B; a fall past 10% is not.
questions.lesson_line: A failure is a shallow break. A deep one is a top that worked.

wrong.Yes; buy the next bounce: At 14% under there is no setup to buy. And buying the first bounce back to the neckline is a named mistake on our card.
wrong.Yes, once back over the neckline: The setup is gone once the fall passes 10% under the neckline. A climb back later does not bring it back.
wrong.No; any close below it kills it: Version B needs at least one close under the neckline. A close under it does not end the setup; a fall past 10% does.

questions.simple: No. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, so the setup is gone.

reasons: the deep-break line is our card's proposed rule

questions.q: Your first sell on a failed-top winner is a fixed third at 3R.
questions.why: False. There's no fixed spot. The first sell is a judgment call. We very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time I wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or somewhere around 5 to 10R, is often best. Sell on a fixed early mark and you cut a winner off before it can run. 3R is a mark on your ruler, not an order.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Day 3 or later, into a push.
questions.simple: False, the first sell is a judgment. It's often into a push of a few days, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: The app's market filter reads Orange, one step from Red. A failed top triggers, but it's not an A+. Do you take it?
questions.why: No. In Orange the market's under pressure, and breakouts fail more often because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best idea there, an A+, the cleanest setup with the tightest risk. Anything less waits. Green is when we press. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Red is mostly cash. Keep this one on your list for when the market gets better.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the pattern. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.No, Orange means all cash: That's closer to Red, and even Red is mostly cash, not all. Orange still lets an A+ through.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Size doesn't fix it. In Orange the question is the grade, and this one isn't an A+.
wrong.Yes, the grade doesn't matter: In Orange the grade is the whole test. Only an A+ gets bought.

questions.simple: No. In an Orange market only an A+ gets bought, and this one isn't an A+.

reasons: rests on the owner's market reading, F65

questions.story: A stock undercut one prior swing low on Tuesday and reclaimed it by Thursday. There is no three-peak top above it and no neckline.
questions.q: What setup is this?
choices: A 2B, bought on the way back
A rounded top with a slow dome
questions.answer: A 2B, bought on the way back
questions.why: A 2B. One swing low broke, and price took it back within a couple of days. That's the whole setup, and the buy comes the moment price reclaims the low. A failed head and shoulders needs a lot more. Three peaks over a neckline, a break, then a wait for the trade over the right-shoulder high. Count the peaks first. No three peaks, no failed head and shoulders.

questions.q: A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought on the reclaim. How soon must the reclaim come?
questions.why: Within 1 to 3 sessions. A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought the moment price reclaims that low. A failed head-and-shoulders is slower: it waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back, then for the trade over the right-shoulder high.

wrong.Within 10 to 15 sessions: Too slow for a 2B. The card gives the reclaim 1 to 3 sessions.
wrong.Within 30 to 40 sessions: That pace belongs to a failed head-and-shoulders, which waits weeks. A 2B reclaims within 1 to 3 sessions.
wrong.Whenever a new base forms: A 2B is not a base. It is bought the moment price reclaims the broken low.

questions.story: A leader broke its neckline, then recovered. The neckline is 98.00 and today it closed at 101.00, back above it. The 50-day is 103.00 and the 200-day is 90.00. The right-shoulder high is 106.00.
questions.q: A friend says to buy it at the close. What do you do?
choices: Buy the close, neckline is support
Half now, half at the trigger
questions.why: Wait. Bracco puts it in two steps: turn the neckline into support, then get back over the 50-day. This one has done step 1. The close at 101.00 is back over the 98.00 neckline, but it's still under the 50-day at 103.00. The 200-day at 90.00 is fine. The buy is the first trade over the 106.00 right-shoulder high, at market during the day, never at the close. Set an alert at 106.00 and wait for it.
questions.lesson_line: Neckline first, then the 50-day. The buy is the trade over the right-shoulder high.
questions.simple: Wait. It's still under the 50-day, and the buy is the trade over the right-shoulder high, not the close.

wrong.Buy the close, neckline is support: Step 1 isn't enough, and we don't buy closes. We buy the trade through the trigger.
wrong.Short it, it's under the 50-day: It's above the 200-day at 90.00, and we never short above the 200-day.
wrong.Half now, half at the trigger: We buy once, at the trigger, with one stop. Half now is just buying early.

questions.story: A stock rallies to 118.00, dips to 109.00, rallies to 118.00 again, dips to 109.00, then rallies to 118.00 a third time. A friend calls it a head and shoulders and wants a failure alert set.
questions.q: Is there a head here?
choices: Yes, three peaks make the shape
Yes, equal peaks are the ideal
Not yet, it needs a fourth peak
questions.why: No head. A head and shoulders needs a middle peak that stands above the other two, and all three of these stop at 118.00. That's a flat top with three bumps, more like a range than a top. Calling every three bumps a head and shoulders is a classic mistake. Set a failure alert on this and you'd be trading a pattern that isn't there.
questions.lesson_line: The head has to be the highest peak. Three equal bumps are a flat top.
questions.simple: No. The middle peak has to be higher than the other two, and these are all equal.

wrong.Yes, three peaks make the shape: Three peaks aren't enough. The middle one has to be the highest.
wrong.Yes, equal peaks are the ideal: Even shoulders are nice. The head still has to stand above them.
wrong.Not yet, it needs a fourth peak: A fourth peak won't create a head that isn't there.

deeper.example: Peter Brandt's warning: novices are way too quick to mislabel market action as a head and shoulders.
